newsitem.title: USA: DC law firm, dealers clash on yield burning study.
newsitem.headline: DC law firm, dealers clash on yield burning study.

text.p: Drafters of a controversial survey on "yield burning" and a spokesman for bond dealers clashed at a key meeting on Tuesday over the survey's validity.

Mary Louise Cohen, whose Washington D.C.-based law firm commissioned the study by economist Steven Feinstein, conceded that data from competitive, rather than negotiated, deals could have "sneaked into" the survey's data base, but it had no significant impact on findings.
And John Phillips, Cohen's partner at Phillips & Cohen, said while the study can be improved, the findings are sound.
"There's a paper trail here," Phillips said. "These numbers are out. The genie is out of the bottle."
The December 1996 survey priced 104 advance refunding escrows and concluded that issuers nationwide face a combined liability of as much as $1 billion because of yield burning.

Phillips, who appeared on a panel at the Government Finance Officers Association's winter meeting, urged the Public Securities Association and bond issuers to work with the firm in coming up with a flawless update of the study.
But Micah Green, executive vice president of PSA, said the study "taints" the municipal bond market unfairly because it was based on responses from only 45 municipalities.

"We will not stand by and let someone taint the market with a broad brush," Green said. He said PSA stands by its testimony at a recent IRS hearing that the Phillips & Cohen study, prepared by Babson College economist Steven Feinstein, has serious methodological flaws.
Bond issuers at GFOA's meeting had a number of questions for the lawyers and Feinstein.
One issuer official complained that she never got the survey, even though Phillips and Cohen stressed it was sent.
Other issuers wanted to know if certain finance advisers or investment providers could be linked with allegedly troubled deals. Feinstein said the sample was not large enough to determine that.
Feinstein issued a detailed "rebuttal" to PSA's charges about the survey, including the association's charge that the survey underestimates the frequency of failed deals.

"Deal failure is extremely rare," Feinstein said. "PSA failed to provide a single example of a failed deal from the 1990-95 period. None of the eight deals cited by PSA were advanced refundings that failed to close during the sample period."
